title: Binding to Element References
text: Now with all these bindings, you hopefully got an overview of how you can work with Svelte and its bindings to conveniently get access to form values. And using 2-way binding here really is extremely helpful, and you'll often use it when working with forms. There is another way of getting access to any element on the page though, so besides using 2-way binding, and also not limited to inputs. Let me first demonstrate it with the help of an input though. Let's say here we have an input and we have a button, and I only need the value once I clicked that button. So here in onClick, I'll trigger saveData, which is a function I have yet to add. So let's do that quickly. Here we have saveData, and I'm not accepting any event object in here because that would be my click event and I'm not interested in that. But I do want to get the text that was entered into this input. Of course, we could set up 2-way binding with bind value and then storing that data which is in that input in some variable. But if I only need this in a read-only way and I never set the value anywhere else, I could do it and it would not be wrong. And in most cases, you will probably do it with 2-way binding, but you can actually also simply read the value from the input. So of course what we could do here is we could console.log document.querySelector and then maybe give this, uh, some ID username. So hashtag username selects by ID. Let's now give this here the ID username so that this is selected. And now we get access to this element, and since it's input element, this will have a value property. And if we do that and we save that all, and I enter super or whatever you want here, and I click save, you see that being printed. This is not the Svelte-ish way of doing it though. This is vanilla JavaScript code which you can use, but there is a more elegant solution. And you might remember that I used a similar approach earlier in the course where I also used querySelector because I had no better tool for the job. Now actually, there is a better tool. You can use binding, but a special form of binding. So instead of relying on selecting this by ID, you can instead add bind, but now you don't bind to value because I don't want 2-way binding, but to this, which is simply a special syntax understood by Svelte. This, this thing here is not a normal attribute you could add to an input. This is simply understood by the Svelte compiler And by binding to this, you can store a reference to that element here, a pointer to that element in a variable of your choice. So now we can add a new variable, usernameInput, for example. And this is the variable which I'll use down there, usernameInput. So now a pointer at this HTML element, or at this DOM element to be precise, is stored in usernameInput. And therefore here in saveData, I can now console.log usernameInput.value because this points at this HTML element. And hence now if I enter super here and I click save, you see that still works. But of course that's way shorter than manually selecting this with querySelector. And we also don't have to add the ID, we can remove that because now this reference and connection is set up behind the scenes by Svelte. Now, this is not 2-way binding. This is really just a pointer at the full element. We're not restricted to reading its value. We can do whatever we want. We can manipulate it, though I would not recommend that. You shouldn't change it programmatically. You should always change your DOM through Svelte by the instructions you place down there. But you can read any data you want. You can check out the CSS classes on the element. You can do whatever you want because if we log it, you'll see it's just the full element. So if I console.log this here and I press save again, it's the full input. By the way, if you want to inspect it here, you can use console.dir, and now you get an inspectable JavaScript object. So this is really the full DOM element, and this does not just work with HTML input elements, it works with any HTML element and your own components as well. So we can also use a div instead and bind this to sumDiv, which of course is a variable I have yet to add. So here is sumDiv. And now for simplicity, when we click Save Data, I can now also console.dir sumDiv. So it's the same button as before, but now I'm binding this here, this div, to the sumDiv variable, and therefore I can now interact with the div and inspect it and do whatever I want. Again, changing something there is not recommended. You should always do that with the help of Svelte's normal syntax, but reading values from it can be really useful.
